questions.q: Using the verified formula total = 2d^2-1, how many total physical qubits does a distance-13 surface code need?
questions.explain: 2(13^2)-1 = 2(169)-1 = 337, computed directly and matching the exercise's table.

questions.q: Why is the qubit-count jump from d=13 to d=17 (240 additional qubits) larger than the jump from d=3 to d=7 (80 additional qubits)?
options: Total qubit count scales quadratically with d, so each fixed step up in distance adds more qubits the larger the starting distance already is
This is an error in the formula; the jumps should be identical
Qubit count only depends on whether d is odd or even, not its actual value
Ancilla qubits stop being added after d=10
questions.explain: Because total qubits grow as 2d^2-1, a quadratic function, equal-sized steps in d produce increasingly larger absolute increases in qubit count at higher distances.

questions.q: In Exercise 2, why does an X error on a data qubit only trigger Z-type stabilizers that include that qubit, not X-type ones?
options: X errors anticommute with Z-type stabilizers but commute with X-type stabilizers, following the same rule used throughout the course since chapter 4
X errors always trigger every stabilizer on the lattice regardless of type
X errors never trigger any stabilizer under any circumstances
X-type stabilizers only exist on bulk qubits, never boundary qubits
questions.explain: This is the same anticommutation rule applied throughout the course: X errors are only detected by Z-type stabilizers that include the affected qubit in their support.

questions.q: Why does a boundary data qubit, touched by fewer stabilizers than a bulk qubit, tend to produce a simpler syndrome pattern when it suffers an error?
options: Fewer stabilizers include the boundary qubit in their support, so fewer (potentially just one) defects appear, making the correction simpler to identify
Boundary qubits are immune to errors entirely
Boundary qubits always trigger all 8 stabilizers on a d=3 lattice simultaneously
Boundary and bulk qubits always produce identical syndrome patterns
questions.explain: Because boundary qubits have smaller stabilizer support (touched by fewer stabilizers), an error there tends to produce fewer defects, which is the easier case for a decoder to resolve, as discussed in the lesson.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe a single-defect case as 'the easy case' for a decoder, in contrast to multiple defects across several rounds?
options: A single defect can be resolved by simply pairing it with the nearest lattice boundary, while multiple defects require the full minimum-weight perfect matching machinery
Single-defect cases are actually impossible and never occur in practice
Decoders cannot handle single-defect cases at all, only multi-defect ones
There is no difference in decoder complexity between single and multiple defects
questions.explain: A lone defect has an obvious correction (pair with the nearest boundary), while multiple defects accumulated across rounds require the general graph-matching approach from lesson 22's MWPM decoder.
